results.title: Codex or Claude wrote my tests — how do I actually trust them? - DEV Community
results.content:
Short answer: don't trust them because they're green. AI writes tests that assert the code's current behavior — including the bugs. Earn the confidence by mutation testing: change the code on purpose and check the tests fail. The ones that stay green are lying to you.

Last month I let Claude generate a test file for a pricing function. Forty tests, all passing, 94% coverage, took ninety seconds. It felt like a gift. Then I changed a `<=` to `<` in the discount tier — a real off-by-one I'd have shipped — and all forty tests still passed. The suite wasn't testing the pricing logic. It was describing it.

That's the trap, and it's specific to generated tests.

## Why AI tests pass against broken code [...] ## Why AI tests pass against broken code

When you write a test, you usually start from "here's what this should do." When a model writes a test, it reads the implementation and writes assertions that match what the code does. Those are not the same job. If the function has a bug, the model faithfully writes a test that locks the bug in place and marks it green.

Three failure patterns show up again and again: [...] Three failure patterns show up again and again:

- The mirror test. It asserts `result == function(input)` essentially by re-deriving the output from the same code path. Tautology. It can never fail.
- The assertion that isn't. `assert response is not None`, `assert len(result) > 0`. Technically an assertion. Catches almost nothing. Models love these because they always pass.
- Coverage theater. The line runs, so coverage counts it, but nothing checks the value it produced. 94% coverage, 0% confidence.

results.title: Codex vs Claude Code: which is the better AI coding agent?
results.content:
Given that the number one complaint I hear about coding agents is running out of credits, Codex has a real edge.

Winner: Codex

## UX and permissions

Codex recognizes a git-tracked repo and is permissive by default. Nice.

Claude Code’s permission system used to drive me crazy — I’d routinely launch it with `--dangerously-skip-permissions`. Anthropic has shipped meaningful improvements since then; the friction has narrowed, though settings still don’t fully persist between sessions in all workflows. Claude Code has also added a VS Code extension, a web IDE for remote control, parallel sessions in the desktop app, and a Cowork feature that extends it beyond just coding. [...] ## Instructions files: Agents.md vs Claude.md

I have a whole separate video and post on writing a good Agents.md. One thing that annoys me about Claude Code is it does not support the Agents.md standard, only Claude.md.

Tools like Cursor, Codex, and Builder.io all support Agents.md. It is annoying to maintain a separate file for Claude when everything else respects the standard.

Winner: Codex

## The big difference: GitHub integration

This is the main reason I prefer Codex.

We tried Claude Code’s GitHub integration briefly. The Builder.io dev team thought it sucked. Reviews were verbose without catching obvious bugs. You could not comment and ask it to fix things in a useful way. It just did not deliver value. [...] Have you tried the Codex CLI or background agents and PR bot? How did it go for you? Drop your experience and tips in the comments.

## Frequently asked questions

Is Codex still better than Claude Code in 2026?

Codex still wins on GitHub integration and pricing. But Claude Code has closed the gap significantly — better UX, a VS Code extension, a web IDE, and Cowork mode. Which is better depends on your workflow. If you live in the terminal and care about GitHub automation, Codex. If you want more configuration options and hooks, Claude Code.

Which should I use if I’m on a budget?

Codex Pro is the better value. More usage at lower cost tiers, and you also get ChatGPT, image generation, and video generation bundled in — not just a coding plan.

results.title: Currents.dev | What's New
results.content:
Playwright tells you what failed. Now Currents tells you why, with AI Failure Analysis. Our specialized agent finds the right root cause nearly 4 times as often as the same model reading only the Playwright output. The agent combines failure information with execution steps, network logs, console logs and test behavior before and after a failure.

- Get the root cause of a failed test without digging through logs
- Get suggested fixes, each with a confidence level
- Watch what the agent checks while it works: the steps, the requests, the screenshots
- Copy the answer into a pull request, an issue or your coding agent's prompt
- Available now on every plan [...] When a test fails, expand Likely cause of the failure in the test's Insights panel. The agent reads the test steps, network logs, console logs and screenshots, and comes back with the type of failure, the root cause in a few sentences, and fixes to try.

### How we tested it

We took CI failures from open-source projects, each with a known fix, and gave each one to the same AI model twice: once with only the Playwright output and the test code, and once through our agent.

Through our agent, the model found the right root cause nearly 4 times as often as with the Playwright output alone, and its first suggested fix addressed the cause 3 times as often.

### Enabling AI Failure Analysis
